exploration.title: Adaptation Island
exploration.subject: Biology
exploration.summary: Predict how inherited shell-color proportions respond when habitat or visual predation changes in a bounded population model.
exploration.question: How can inherited variation and unequal survival change a population across generations?
exploration.explanation: Natural selection requires heritable variation and differences in survival or reproduction. In this fictional population, visual predators give the better-camouflaged shell variant a larger relative survival-and-descendant weight. The resulting expected proportions change across generations, but individuals retain their shell color. The deterministic 0.9 and 0.5 weights are invented teaching values, not measured probabilities. The model normalizes the population to 100% and omits genes and mating, mutation, migration, random drift, population-size change and other traits.

experiments.title: Compare habitats
experiments.instruction: Predict whether the same inherited variation reaches the same proportions on dark and pale ground. Start both trials at 50% dark and 50% pale with predators and identical invented weights; change only ground color and compare exactly five generations.
experiments.observe: Dark ground gives 95.0% dark and 5.0% pale; pale ground gives 5.0% dark and 95.0% pale. Explain the reversal through environment-dependent differential survival, not individuals changing color.

experiments.title: Remove predation
experiments.instruction: Predict whether proportions change when both variants have equal weights. Keep dark ground, a 50/50 start and five generations fixed; change only predation.
experiments.observe: Predation with unequal 0.9/0.5 weights gives 95.0% dark. Without predation, both weights are 0.9 and proportions remain 50.0% dark and 50.0% pale. Explain why inherited variation alone does not favor either variant.

exploration.misconception: Natural selection does not plan ahead or make an individual acquire a needed trait. It changes populations when existing heritable variants differ in survival or descendant contribution under particular conditions.
